Have Got to and Going to Have to for What Is Necessary (Negative Form)
“Have got to” and “going to have” in their negative forms both represent the idea that something is not necessary, but in different moments in time.

HAVE GOT TO
When you use “have got to” in the negative form, the idea that something is not necessary to do arises. You use it for mentioning that there is no need to proceed in a specific way regarding a situation.
The structure that you need to follow to create negative sentences is:  Subject + have/has + not + got to + verb (base form) + complement.

For example,
These systems haven't got to be ready tomorrow, but today!
He hasn't got to include calculations in the system.

GOING TO HAVE TO
“Going to have to” represents the same idea as the form “have got to”; however, it implies that the action to be taken is required to happen at some point or moment in the future.
The structure that you need to follow is as follows:  Subject + am/is/are + not + going to have to + verb (base form) + complement.

For example,
You are not going to have to fix that bug now.
She is not going to have to check the data manipulation in the system.
You haven't got to forget that they have been known as quality attributes too as they make reference to aspects like security, privacy and legislative requirements.
You are not going to have to do much, just check the functional and non-functional requirements of this new system before we launch it.
Within the systems engineering, functional and non-functional requirements work together in order to make systems or products operate.
The objectives that a product or system aims to achieve are specifically represented, among others, by the functional and non-functional requirements.

FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
Within the functional requirements, information related to the functions and activities that the system or product has to perform in specific situations is detailed. In other words, elements such as the input, output, and actual performance of a system concern this field. Furthermore, the functional requirements are not written using technical language as everybody must understand them.

What you find in the functional requirement information is basically descriptions regarding the operations that the system or product performs, such as the work-flow of the system, reports, and regulatory requirements.

NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
Contrary to the functional requirements, the non-functional requirements depict the operation of a system which is ruled by the system architecture. The functional requirement illustrates what a system has to do and react in specific situations, whereas the non-functional requirements illustrate how this system has to be.

The non-functional requirements, or quality attributes, are reflected on elements like the timing, the application domain of the system, the legislative, privacy, safety and ethical requirements as well as the interoperability.

images.text:
Sarah: Here, this is this week's task. You are not going to have to do much, just check the functional and non-functional requirements of this new system before we launch it.
Peter: Wait! What are those?
Sarah: You've got to be kidding. You have worked on that for weeks! The functional requirements are those that define what the system has to do in specific situations. In other words, that's the one that states the way the input, output and real performance of a system work together and produce a desired outcome. You're not going to have to focus on other aspects that are not the function of the system and its compliance with the specific objective of the product.

Peter: Got it! What about the other requirement?
Sarah: Once you've assessed the non-functional requirements, you have to make sure they have evidenced the overall operation of the system; in other words, the way the system has to be. You haven't got to forget that you knew them as quality attributes too as they made reference to aspects like security, privacy and legislative requirements.
Peter: I haven't got to forget that!

Sarah: Exactly, you definitely haven't got to confuse those two requirements. Let me give some examples. Within the functional requirements, you are not going to have to find other aspects that are not the descriptions of the operations, which the system performs in given cases as well as the reports and the workflow of the system. On the other hand, the non-functional requirements haven't got to focus on what happens in specific situations but on the legislative, privacy, safety, and ethical requirements of the system. You're not going to have to learn their definitions but to identify the cases you encounter.
